tool.name: LSRIOnContourPolylines

summary.para:
View online help files: https://www.jennessent.com/topographic-analysis/lsri-on-contours.html
Computes the Land Surface Ruggedness Index (LSRI), or Beasom's Ruggedness Index, directly from an existing contour (or any polyline) feature class: the total length of polyline within a circular neighborhood of each cell (Beasom, Wiggers, and Giardino 1983). Higher values mean more, or more convoluted, line nearby, i.e. more rugged terrain. If the input has a selection, only the selected features are used.

tool.usage:
Beasom, Wiggers, and Giardino (1983) found that land surface ruggedness is closely related to the total length of contour lines crossing a fixed-size sample area -- a rugged, broken landscape needs many, tightly-spaced, winding contour lines to represent it, while a smooth or gently-rolling landscape needs few, widely-spaced, nearly-straight ones. They measured that total length directly with a tracing wheel over a 40-hectare circular sample area for a validation subset, but for routine use on many areas proposed a faster manual proxy instead: a dot-grid transparency laid over a printed topographic map, counting how many dots fell on a contour line (their "Land Surface Ruggedness Index"). That dot-counting shortcut only made sense because manually tracing every contour line by hand was tedious -- it does not apply here. This tool automates the more accurate of Beasom et al.'s two methods, the direct length measurement, over a moving circular neighborhood instead of a single fixed sample area, so you get a continuous ruggedness surface rather than one value per plot, with no need for the dot-grid estimate.
This tool works from an existing polyline feature class -- typically elevation contours generated some other way, but any polyline data works. If you want to generate contours from a DEM and compute LSRI in one step, use the companion LSRI on DEM tool instead, which can also save its derived contours as a feature class for use here. If the input feature class (or layer) has an active selection, only the selected features are measured, the standard ArcGIS Pro behavior for a Feature Layer input.
This tool is similar in spirit to Esri's Line Density tool, which also measures linear features within a circular neighborhood of each cell -- but Line Density reports a density (length per unit area), while this tool reports the total length directly, matching Beasom et al.'s original ruggedness concept. The two are not computed from each other; this tool measures polyline length independently, using its own exact (non-rasterized) calculation.
This tool works on both projected and geographic (latitude/longitude) polyline data. On geographic data, the neighborhood radius and the length it measures are computed as true ground (geodesic) distances, on the input's reference spheroid -- not a raw, misleading degree-space distance -- so results are correct at any latitude. The only approximation is the Cells radius unit, which uses a single representative ground cell size (at the data's own center latitude) rather than one that varies across the extent; Meters, Kilometers, Feet, and Miles radius units need no such approximation.

dialogReference.para: The polyline features to compute LSRI from -- typically elevation contours, but any polyline data works. Both projected and geographic (latitude/longitude) coordinate systems are supported. If the input has an active selection, only the selected features are used.
The output LSRI raster (floating point): the total length of polyline within the neighborhood radius of each cell, in the chosen length units. A suggested name is filled in from the input.
The cell size of the output raster, in the input's map units. Defaults to the greater of the input feature class's width or height, divided by 1000.

How far the neighborhood extends around each cell, in the radius units below. There is no default -- choose a radius appropriate to the landscape scale and research question you're examining. (Beasom et al. used 40-hectare sample plots, a radius of about 356.8 meters, and do not say why; it was probably a practical size to trace by hand on a printed 7.5-minute topographic map -- a paper-map constraint that doesn't apply to a computed neighborhood, so this tool does not impose that scale on you.) Larger values examine ruggedness at a coarser landscape scale.
The units of the radius. Cells applies a radius of that many output cells (using the cell size above). Meters, Kilometers, Feet, and Miles are converted to the input's map units.
The linear units the output LSRI values are reported in (total polyline length within the neighborhood). Default is Meters.

scriptExample.title: LSRI on Contours example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: LSRI using a 500-meter neighborhood radius, from an existing contour feature class.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.LSRIOnContourPolylines( in_polylines=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_Contours", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\Contours_LSRI", cell_size=30, radius=500, radius_units="Meters", length_units="Meters")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Land Surface Ruggedness Index (LSRI), or Beasom's Ruggedness Index, computed directly from an existing contour (or any polyline) feature class: total polyline length within a circular neighborhood of each cell (Beasom, Wiggers, and Giardino 1983).
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Computes, for each output cell, the total length of polyline falling within a circular neighborhood of an existing contour (or any polyline) feature class -- the Land Surface Ruggedness Index of Beasom, Wiggers, and Giardino (1983), automating the more accurate of the two methods they describe (direct length measurement) rather than their manual dot-grid proxy. If the input has an active selection, only the selected features are used. Implemented independently of Esri's Line Density tool (which reports a related but different quantity, density rather than total length), using an exact segment/circle-clip length calculation, not a rasterized approximation -- computed as true geodesic ground distance (via 3-D ECEF coordinates on the reference spheroid) on geographic data, so it is correct at any latitude, not just an approximation. The default cell size is the greater of the input's width or height, divided by 1000. The output is floating point and carries statistics and a histogram; pyramids are built with bilinear resampling.
